GK-12.c01: A **traffic emergency** is two vehicles about to collide; a **vehicle emergency** is a tire, brake or other critical part failing.
Safe driving helps prevent emergencies, and your chance of avoiding a crash depends on how well you act.
GK-12.c02: **Stopping is not always safest**: turning away almost always takes less time than stopping a heavy truck.
Keep **both hands on the wheel** at all times, **don't brake while turning**, turn only as much as needed, and be ready to countersteer.
If an oncoming driver drifts into your lane, **move right**; right is often best when the shoulder is clear or both sides are blocked.
Leaving the road, avoid braking until you slow to about **20 mph**, and keep one set of wheels on the pavement if you can.
To return before stopping, turn sharply (don't edge back), then **countersteer immediately** once both front tires are on pavement.
GK-12.c03: **Controlled braking** means braking as hard as possible without locking the wheels, with very small steering moves.
**Stab braking** means brake fully, release when the wheels lock, and brake again once they roll; wheels may need **up to 1 second**.
Stab braking is **only for vehicles WITHOUT ABS**.
**Don't jam on the brakes**, because locked wheels mean a skid you cannot control.
GK-12.c04: Most hydraulic brake failures have **2 causes**: loss of hydraulic pressure and brake fade on long hills.
If the pedal is spongy or goes to the floor, **downshift**, **pump the brakes**, and use the parking brake while holding its release.
If brakes fail on a downgrade, **use an escape ramp**; if none, take the least dangerous route, such as an open field or uphill road.
**Act as soon as you know** the brakes don't work, because every second the truck gets faster.
GK-12.c05: Signs of tire failure are a loud **bang** (assume it was yours), heavy vibration, **heavy steering** (front tire), or fishtailing (rear tire).
**Hold the steering wheel firmly**, because a failed front tire can twist it out of your hands.
**Stay off the brake** and let the truck slow first, then brake very gently, pull off, and check all tires.
GK-12.c06: **ABS** uses a computer to **prevent wheel lockup** during hard braking, working on top of your regular brakes.
It switches on only when a wheel is about to lock, and its job is **control, not a shorter stop**.
GK-12.c07: **Sensors** detect a wheel about to lock, and the **ECU** lowers brake pressure on that wheel.
It gives the **most braking possible without lockup**, reacting far faster than any driver; otherwise the brakes work normally.
GK-12.c08: ABS is required on **truck tractors with air brakes** built on or after **March 1, 1997**.
ABS is required on **all other air-brake vehicles** (buses, trucks, trailers, converter dollies) built on or after **March 1, 1998**.
ABS is required on hydraulic-brake trucks and buses of **10,000 lb or more** GVWR built on or after **March 1, 1999**.
GK-12.c09: Tractors, trucks and buses have a **yellow** ABS malfunction lamp on the instrument panel; trailers have one on the **left side**, front or rear corner.
The lamp lights at start-up then goes out; on older systems it may stay on until you exceed **5 mph**.
A lamp that **stays on** after the bulb check or lights while driving means you may have **lost ABS control**.
On older towed units, look underneath for an **ECU** box and wheel-speed sensor wires.
GK-12.c10: Without ABS, locked **steering wheels** mean lost steering; other locked wheels can cause a **skid, jackknife, or spin**.
With ABS you **may or may not stop faster**, but you should be able to **steer around an obstacle while braking**.
GK-12.c11: Even ABS on only the tractor, only the trailer, or a single axle improves control, so **brake normally**.
**Tractor-only ABS**: watch the trailer and **ease off the brakes** if it starts to swing out.
**Trailer-only ABS**: if you lose steering or the tractor starts to jackknife, **ease off the brakes** until back in control.
GK-12.c12: Brake the way you always have, using **only as much force as you need** for a safe, controlled stop.
Brake the same way whether ABS is on the bus, tractor, trailer or both, and back off if needed to stay in control.
Exception: with **working ABS on ALL axles**, you may **brake fully** in an emergency stop.
GK-12.c13: Without ABS you **still have your normal brakes**, so drive and brake as usual.
A lamp that stays on or lights while driving means lost ABS on **1 or more wheels**; **get it repaired soon**.
GK-12.c14: ABS is **no excuse** for more speed, shorter following distance, or careless driving.
ABS does **not** stop power skids or turning skids; it should stop skids and jackknifes **caused by braking**.
ABS will **not necessarily shorten** stopping distance and doesn't change your ultimate stopping power.
Worn or poorly maintained brakes are still bad brakes, and a careful **driver** remains the most important safety feature.
GK-12.c15: A **skid** happens when the tires stop gripping the road.
The **4 causes** are over-braking (including a speed retarder on slippery roads), over-steering, over-acceleration, and driving too fast.
**Driving too fast** causes most serious skids.
GK-12.c16: **Drive-wheel skids** are by far the most common, when rear drive wheels lose grip from hard braking or too much throttle.
For an acceleration skid on ice or snow, **take your foot off the accelerator**; if very slippery, also **push in the clutch**.
A locked wheel grips less than a rolling one, so a bus or straight truck may **spin out** and a tractor-trailer may **jackknife**.
GK-12.c17: First **stop braking** so the rear wheels roll again and stop sliding.
Then **countersteer** quickly the other way as the vehicle straightens, or you will skid in the **opposite direction**.
These skills need practice, and a large driving range or **skid pad** is the best place to learn them.
GK-12.c18: Front-wheel skids are most often caused by **driving too fast for conditions**, plus worn front tread or too little front-axle weight.
The front end keeps going **straight** no matter how much you turn the wheel.
**The only fix is to let the vehicle slow down**: stop turning so sharply and/or braking so hard, without starting a new skid.
